title: The Death of Vertical Software
summary: Why Rigid Systems Are Losing in Modern Logistics
body_text: Vertical software was supposed to be the answer. Built specifically for industries like logistics, it promised to simplify operations, encode best practices, and deliver plug-and-play efficiency. But for many transportation companies, it hasn’t played out that way. Instead, vertical software has become a bottleneck. Rigid workflows, slow innovation, and a disconnect from how operators actually work have led many operations and technology leaders to question whether the tools designed “for them” truly serve them anymore. How Vertical Software Rose to Power The idea was simple: instead of customizing a horizontal system to fit logistics workflows, what if you just bought a system built for trucking, brokerages, or warehousing out of the box? That gave rise to vertical software platforms like TMSs and WMSs that promised domain-specific features, regulatory alignment, and built-in best practices. Vendors pitched these systems as pre-fit suits: you wouldn’t need to tailor them, just put them on and start running. For a while, that worked. Especially in the early days of SaaS, when industry-specific functionality was rare, a vertical tool that understood LTL vs. FTL or freight rating logic was a big deal. But like any pre-fit suit, it only works if you fit the mold. Why That Model Is Breaking If we learned anything in our 10 years of building TMSes, modern logistics isn’t one-size-fits-all. Operations evolve fast and strategies differ. A brokerage specializing in expedited freight looks nothing like a mid-sized carrier. Yet most vertical systems are still designed around a single way of doing things. That means if your workflows don’t match the software’s assumptions, you either: Force your team to conform to the tool Build painful workarounds Or give up and revert to spreadsheets None of those are good enough. Even worse, many vertical tools aren’t built to be easily adapted. Because they were designed to be prescriptive, their flexibility is limited. You’ll often hear users say things like: “We wanted to use the TMS for this workflow, but it doesn’t support multi-leg loads with variable rate structures, so we still track those separately.” That’s how shelfware happens. The Failure Rate Problem It’s not just theory. The failure rates for vertical software implementations are alarming: Over 70% of digital transformation projects (including ERP and logistics system rollouts) fail to meet objectives (McKinsey, 2020). In transportation, implementation failure often stems from workflows not matching the tool and low user adoption The most common cause? The software didn’t fit how the business actually works. The Illusion of Best Practices Vertical vendors love to talk about built-in best practices. But here’s the truth: there’s no universal best practice in logistics. Every operation has its edge cases, exceptions, and tribal knowledge. When software assumes there is one “right” way to run a load or invoice a customer, it ends up creating friction instead of removing it. This is the same problem AI tools face when they lack context. They guess. And in logistics, guessing leads to bad calls. What Operators Actually Need What logistics leaders want isn’t a rigid system that tells them how to run. They want a platform that: Understands their existing workflows Lets them customize processes without code Can evolve as their business changes Embeds intelligence that sees the full picture In other words, software that adapts to the business, not the other way around. That’s what modern TMS platforms like Rose Rocket are built around. Rather than locking you into someone else’s assumptions, they deploy into your environment, learn how your business actually runs, and support the workflows that matter most. The Future: Contextual Platforms, Not Prescriptive Suites The death of vertical software doesn’t mean the end of industry-specific tooling. It means the end of inflexible, prescriptive systems that can’t keep up with operational reality. The winners in logistics tech will be platforms that are: Context-aware Configurable without complexity Grounded in real operations, not imagined best practices Because in a world where agility is everything, rigidity is a liability. It’s time to stop working around software, and start working with software that works around you .

title: 5 Best Fuel Cards for New Businesses
summary: Explore the best fuel cards for new businesses and small fleets. Learn about AtoB's fleet card approval requirements, discounts, and features today.
body_text: Most fuel card providers are built for established operations with strong business credit profiles. New businesses can still qualify through prepaid options and cash flow-based underwriting. We cover the best fuel cards for early-stage carriers, what to evaluate, and how to apply with limited documentation. Providers like AtoB offer both credit and prepaid fuel cards designed for businesses at every stage, including startups with no established credit history. Why New Businesses Need a Fuel Card New businesses that rely on vehicles face a critical decision: use personal credit cards for fuel or invest in a dedicated fuel card. While business credit cards are available, they often mix personal and business expenses, offer limited controls, and do not provide the tools needed for fleet management. A fuel card, by contrast, is designed specifically for operational use. Here is what a fuel card offers: Centralize fuel expenses across drivers and vehicles Track and manage fuel purchases through a single portal Control spending with built-in limits and restrictions Simplify IFTA fuel tax reporting and reduce administrative work Improve fuel efficiency by supporting fuel-efficient driving habits If you are a new business owner, separating fuel expenses early creates better financial visibility and reduces the need for reimbursement tracking across your employees. What to Look for in a Fuel Card as a New Business New businesses have different needs than established fleets. The right solution should align with early-stage operations while still scaling as the business grows. Acceptance Network and Spending Controls Cards with universal acceptance provide the most flexibility. Solutions that work nationwide allow drivers to fuel at major truck stops, independent gas stations, and locations near job sites. Spending controls matter more when processes are still forming. Look for features that allow you to: Restrict spending to fuel-only purchases Set limits per transaction or per driver Block purchases at non-fuel merchants Track activity in real time These tools help control spending and reduce the risk of misuse. Credit vs. Prepaid and Fee Transparency Choose between different fuel card types based on your business stage: Credit cards - Function like charge cards with a credit line and billing cycle Prepaid cards - The best prepaid fuel cards are ideal for brand-new operations or those with limited credit history Evaluate fees carefully. Common charges to watch for include setup fees, monthly per-card charges, per-transaction fees, out-of-network penalties, and late payment costs. Some cards advertise no monthly fee but charge per transaction. Understanding the full cost helps ensure the card is a fit for your business. Business Credit Reporting and IFTA Compliance A fuel card that reports to business credit bureaus helps build a financial profile over time. This is important for businesses that plan to apply for financing later. New carriers also need IFTA-ready reporting. Look for these features: Itemized transaction data - Detailed purchase records with location and gallons Digital receipt capture - Automatic receipt storage and organization Automated IFTA exports - Pre-formatted reports for quarterly filing Accounting software integration - Direct sync with QuickBooks or similar platforms These features reduce administrative work and improve accuracy. Best Fuel Cards for New Businesses These fleet fuel cards for small business operations offer realistic approval paths, evaluated on accessibility, fees, savings potential, and credit-building features. Data as of 05/05/2026 *Check provider websites for the most up-to-date information regarding their offerings Factor Easy Approval Fuel Cards Standard Business Credit Cards Approval Requirements Minimal or no credit check Good to excellent business credit Typical Credit Limits Lower or prefunded Higher limits Rewards Fuel discounts, limited cash back Cash back on purchases, rewards points Fees Lower or transparent Varies by provider but may include high annual fees Controls Strong fleet management tools Limited controls How to Apply for a Fuel Card as a New Business Preparation improves approval odds even with limited documentation and credit history, especially for businesses exploring easy approval business gas cards as an entry point into fleet financing. What You Will Need Most card issuers require: EIN - Your Employer Identification Number from the IRS Business formation documents - LLC articles of organization or corporate registration Valid driver's license - Government-issued ID for the primary account holder Business bank account - Required by some providers for verification Bank statements - Showing recent revenue history for credit-based applications Strengthening a Thin Application and the Approval Timeline Steps to improve your application: Register as an LLC or corporation rather than a sole proprietorship Open a dedicated business bank account separate from personal finances Ensure business information matches across all registrations and documents Compare secured vs prepaid fuel cards and consider starting with a prefunded option to establish payment history first Prepaid cards typically receive approval within one to two business days. Credit-based fleet cards may take several days, depending on underwriting requirements. Fees and Costs New Businesses Should Watch For Fee structures vary significantly across issuers and can erode savings for businesses on thin margins. Common Fee Types Watch for these charges: Setup and onboarding fees Monthly account charges Transaction fees for fuel purchases Fees for out-of-network fueling Evaluate savings carefully. Even small discounts on fuel prices can add up, but only if fees do not offset those benefits. Calculating True Cost vs. Savings Calculate net savings: monthly fuel volume multiplied by per-gallon discount, minus total monthly fees. Cards advertising large discounts within small networks often deliver less real-world savings than cards with broad acceptance and moderate discounts. This is a key factor when evaluating fleet fuel cards with discounts across different operating routes. How Fuel Cards Help New Businesses Grow A fuel card does more than pay for fuel. It becomes part of your financial infrastructure. Building Business Credit from Day One Consistent on-time payments on a fuel card that reports to business credit bureaus creates a credit profile over time, which is essential for building business credit for fleet owners . This history unlocks better financing for equipment, vehicles, and working capital. AtoB reports to Experian for both credit and prepaid cards, making it one of the few providers offering credit building even on a prefunded product. Scaling from Fuel Card to Fleet Financial Platform As operations expand, the right provider grows with you. Business credit cards, driver payroll, bill pay, fleet banking, and working capital can be consolidated under one platform, reducing vendor count and simplifying fleet expense management. AtoB's fleet spend management platform exemplifies this growth path, supporting fleets from startup through scale. ‍ Fuel Cards for New Businesses FAQs Can a brand-new business get a fuel card? Yes. Prepaid fuel cards require no credit check, credit history, or personal guarantee. Credit-based options may require several months of revenue history, but often use cash flow-based underwriting. What is the best fleet fuel card for a small business? Finding the best fuel card for small business operations depends on fleet size, routes, and credit profile. For new and small businesses, AtoB offers nationwide Mastercard acceptance, both credit and prepaid options, transparent pricing, and business credit reporting through its gas cards for businesses . How long does it take to get approved for a fuel card? Prepaid fuel cards typically receive approval within one to two business days. Credit-based fleet cards may take several days, depending on underwriting requirements. Do fuel cards help build business credit? Some do, but not all. Look for business fuel cards that report to credit bureaus like Experian or Dun & Bradstreet. AtoB reports for both credit and prepaid cards. Start Managing Fuel Costs from Day One The right fuel card gives new fleets immediate access to fuel discounts, spending controls, and business credit building. You do not need years of operating history or a personal guarantee to get started. AtoB is purpose-built for businesses at every stage, offering both credit and prepaid fuel cards with broad acceptance and a platform that grows with your fleet. title: Best Practices for Cleaning Warehouse and Logistics Environments
summary: Discover smart cleaning solutions for warehouses to boost safety, efficiency, and compliance with robotic scrubbers and advanced equipment
body_text: May 13, 2025 7:43 AM by Tennant Company Posted in Cleaning Solutions , Productivity , Best Practices , Robotic Cleaning Machines , Cleaning Challenges , Warehouse managers juggle numerous responsibilities—ensuring efficient operations, maintaining worker safety, and optimizing productivity. One often-overlooked factor that impacts all three is cleanliness. But with heavy foot traffic, high-volume machinery, and strict safety requirements, maintaining a clean and safe environment in industrial warehouses or huge logistic facilities can feel like an uphill battle. The solution? Smart cleaning strategies and efficient cleaning technologies that support productivity, enhance safety, and help warehouse managers stay ahead in a competitive industry. Why Cleanliness is important in Warehouses and Logistics? Industrial and logistic facilities are uniquely demanding environments, with a mix of high-traffic zones, heavy-duty equipment, and hard-to-reach spaces. From warehouse floors to loading docks, cleanliness is about more than appearances—it directly impacts your operational efficiency, plays a critical role in preventing accidents, reducing downtime, and keeping operations compliant with industry standards. Operational impact : Dirt and debris on warehouse floors can damage forklifts, conveyor belts, and automated systems, leading to unexpected downtime and repair costs. At the same time, the presence of dust and debris can slow down machinery productivity and worker operations, causing additional inefficiencies. Safety concerns : Spills, dust, and clutter can cause slips, trips, and falls— one of the most common workplace injuries in warehouses, often caused by wet or unclean floors. Even dust can be a serious problem in logistic environments, as poor air quality from dust buildup can lead to respiratory problems and increased sick days among staff. Compliance and morale : Clean warehouses reflect a commitment to safety and professionalism, which, not only ensures regulatory compliance, but also boosts employee morale. Smart Cleaning Solutions for Warehouse Managers Implementing efficient cleaning practices doesn’t have to be overwhelming. With the right strategies and advanced cleaning technologies , such as robotic scrubbers , you can ensure a safer and more productive work environment. 1. Choose equipment that meets the unique needs of your facility From expansive warehouse floors to narrow loading docks, up to parking lots, industrial cleaning equipment needs to be versatile and efficient to address a wide range of challenges. Large-scale cleaning : Industrial floor scrubbers with wide cleaning paths are ideal for quickly tackling dirt and grime in high-traffic areas. When dealing with dust and heavy debris, powerful industrial sweepers , such as Tennant 800 , can support your indoor or outdoor cleaning operations. Compact efficiency : Smaller, maneuverable floor scrubbers, such as Tennant i-mop® Lite or i-mop® XL Plus , are perfect for navigating tight spaces, such as narrow aisles and storage zones, ensuring even hard-to-reach areas stay clean. Heavy-duty power : High-performance sweeper-scrubbers are essential for handling tough jobs, like removing dirt and debris from parking lots and loading bays, where conditions can be especially demanding. This flexibility ensures that every corner of a logistics or warehousing facility can be cleaned effectively and efficiently, no matter the size or type of space. 2. Rely on Automation and Robotic Cleaning Machines Robotic Floor Scrubbers are an effective first step in integrating autonomy into your business: Tennant robotic equipment is powered by BrainOS®, an advanced artificial intelligence and robotic technology platform that ensures safe, accurate navigation. Consistent and instant results : Robotic cleaning machines offer effective and high-quality cleaning with the ability to operate seamlessly alongside your team, ensuring floors are consistently cleaned while reducing the need for manual labor. Advanced safety features : Robotic scrubbers, like the Tennant T16AMR , are equipped with sensors like LiDAR and 3D cameras to navigate obstacles safely, protecting employees and equipment alike. Sustainable solutions : With Tennant’s ec-H20 NanoClean® technology , you can minimize chemical usage while achieving a deeper clean—helping you stay environmentally responsible. 3. Scheduled Cleaning Protocols Consistency is key when maintaining cleanliness. Implementing a structured cleaning schedule ensures that critical areas are addressed regularly: Daily : Sweep and scrub high-traffic areas, empty trash bins, and check for spills. Weekly : Deep-clean floors and sanitize common areas. Monthly : Conduct a full warehouse inspection, clean air vents, and assess the effectiveness of cleaning procedures. 4. Employee Involvement & Training Cleanliness is also a team effort. Educate staff on best practices and encourage responsibility by training employees around proper disposal, establishing a culture of accountability, or even by implementing a reward system that prizes those who consistently uphold cleanliness standards. A Cleaner Warehouse is a Safer Warehouse Warehouse managers who prioritize cleanliness not only create a safer work environment, but also improve efficiency, reduce maintenance costs, and enhance employee morale. Investing in smart cleaning solutions is not just about hygiene—it’s about long-term operational success. By integrating robotic technology, structured cleaning protocols, and employee engagement, you can maintain a warehouse that runs smoothly, efficiently, and safely. Ready to optimize your warehouse cleaning strategy? Contact us today to schedule a demonstration. Our cleaning technologies are designed to tackle industrial and logistic cleaning challenges head-on—all while delivering the reliability you need in a fast-paced industry. title: An Intro to Nesting
summary: Material waste eats away at a fab's margins. We describe how to minimize this with effective nesting.
body_text: What's the Problem? Structural steel fabricators lose money on every inch of metal stock wasted. Even on a small job, metal waste can clear a few thousand dollars from your margin. This adds up over the course of a year. Fabs fight this through efficient nesting, the art of getting the minimum metal needed for their cuts. What's Nesting? Nesting is how cuts are planned on stock pieces. Stock pieces are the lengths of steel (usually 20', 40' or 60') purchased from the metal manufacturer, supplier, or distributor. Nesting is how to cut out usable pieces from these stock pieces. The challenge: Do this accurately : there can be dozens to thousands of different beams and columns to cut. Nothing should be forgotten. Do this fast : by-hand nesting for dozens of beams is time consuming. Thousands is impossible. Do this efficiently : wasted material is wasted spend. To do this efficiently, we introduce the idea of a pattern . A pattern is the collection of cuts made on a stock piece. A fab might want to cut two 15' beams and one 10' beam. Consider one pattern on a 40' stock vs 3 patterns on three pieces of 20' stock for doing this. Pattern Waste Comparison: 40' vs 20' Stock Stock Length Pattern Drop Waste 40' x1 Stock 1: 15', 15', 10' 0' 0' 20' x3 Stock 1: 15' Stock 2: 15' Stock 3: 10' Stock 1: 5' Stock 2: 5' Stock 3: 10' 20' We can see different patterns on different stock lead to different waste. As the amount of stocks and cuts grows, it gets harder and harder to figure out which pattern is the most efficient. There are over a dozen different wide flange shapes in this framing plan snippet, with many different lengths. Multiply that across multiple floors in this med center—the number of cuts and lengths to track can be over a hundred, and this can lead to over a million possible patterns. In addition to choosing the stock lengths and pattern, the following considerations are also important: Kerf , or how much metal is lost per cut. End trim , or how much static length we need on the end of the beam to hold the piece steady while cutting. So, available stock lengths, kerf, and end trim are all factors in finding the right patterns to cut your steel. For a given job there could be just a few patterns, but often there are thousands or millions. This makes finding an efficient pattern like searching for a needle in a haystack. It's worth it, if done fast enough. Money is on the line! Practical Nesting In practice, nesting will be done through software, since that's the only way to get through the thousands or millions of patterns efficiently. So you know you need stock lengths, cuts, kerf, and end trim, which is what every software will ask of you. We'll briefly cover how to choose these. Then we'll cover tips for effective nesting. Stock lengths : these are provided by whoever you're buying from. Often, allowing your nesting software to use longer stock makes for less waste. Cuts : these will come from your plans and schematics. Kerf : different cutting methods will yield different kerf. The manufacturer of your cutting device (e.g., plasma vs saw) should have recommended kerf allowances. Follow your manufacturer's guidance. Free guides are also available online here , here , and here . End Trim : this is going to depend on your machine. Your machine may "grip" part of the stock and that cannot be advanced past the saw—this is lost length that cannot be used and hence should be accounted for when nesting. Again, your machine manufacturer should have guidance. With these in mind, you can start nesting. This is the minimum to start nesting in any software. The more material you put into the nesting, the more ways the software can figure out how to organize the cuts to minimize waste. Some pitfalls to avoid, as well: Pitfall 1 : Check if that large beam is actually 70', or if it is composed of small splices! If the 70' beam is actually several smaller pieces welded or bolted together, then the nesting only needs the smaller splices. Pitfall 2 : Make sure the beams you order are the size you can have delivered. Are you able to rent a big enough truck to get that 60' stock on the highway? Pitfall 3 : Double check your beam measurements. If your cut is too small, you might run out of space on your stock length. With this in mind, you're ready to save money with nesting. But how? Getting Started Your options are to nest by-hand, ask a distributor to nest for you, or use your own software. We'll cover each, but we recommend using your own software. You can try to nest by-hand, but that is challenging beyond a few sticks. To nest by hand, you'd have to sit down, take a stock length, and fit what you can. If you can't fit something, either pull up a new stick or go up a stock size. Hope that in the drop you can fit something so you don't waste material. But just getting workable patterns for every stick could take hours. Sometimes, mistakes are made—pieces are dropped or time is lost. This was painful enough that mathematicians Gilmore and Gomory came up with an early algorithm in 1961 . These modern nesting algorithms were first implemented in an early software in 1984 by ProNest. What could take hours or days now happens in seconds. You can have distributors nest for you, but sometimes that means you miss out. How so? Some fabs see considerable savings by using larger stock lengths, but the distributor or supplier might not sell those—the distributor is going to sell whatever works for them. Instead, you can go right to the mill and get a better deal. As a bonus, the mill is often cheaper on a per-foot basis anyways (though you'll usually have to wait an extra day for delivery). You'll only know if you can save cash if you nest yourself. Today, nesting by software is all but mandatory—it's priced into many jobs and expected by GCs.
